exp: A car moving much slower than the flow causes tailgating and unsafe passing. Most states ban driving so slowly that you block normal traffic.
src: State minimum speed laws; California Driver Handbook, Navigating the Roads, https://www.dmv.ca.gov/portal/handbook/california-driver-handbook/navigating-the-roads/

q: During perception and reaction time, what is your car doing?
a: Still moving at full speed
b: Slowing down quickly
c: Standing still
d: Skidding
exp: The car does not slow until you press the brake, so it keeps going at the same speed while you notice and react.
src: State driver manuals, stopping distance

q: Which of these makes your braking distance longer?
a: A dry road surface
b: A wet road surface
c: Driving uphill
d: Driving slower
exp: Wet, icy or loose surfaces give the tires less grip, so the car needs more distance to stop.
src: PennDOT Driver's Manual, Managing Space, https://www.pa.gov/agencies/dmv/driver-services/pennsylvania-drivers-manual/online-drivers-manual/everyday-driving-skills/managing-space

q: Which of these makes your perception and reaction distance longer?
a: Driving on a dry road
b: Having new tires
c: Driving uphill
d: Being tired or distracted
exp: Fatigue, distraction, alcohol and drugs slow the time it takes you to notice a hazard and hit the brake.
src: NHTSA Distracted Driving, https://www.nhtsa.gov/risky-driving/distracted-driving

q: At night, how fast should you drive in relation to your headlights?
a: At the posted limit, whatever you can see
b: Fast enough to keep up with the car ahead
c: Slow enough to stop within the distance your headlights light up
d: Slow enough to stop within twice your headlight range
exp: You should always be able to stop within the distance you can see clearly. At night that is the reach of your headlights.
src: State driver manuals, night driving and speed

q: You are counting your following distance and you reach the fixed point before you finish the count. What should you do?
a: Ease off the gas to open the gap
b: Change lanes right away
c: Flash your headlights
d: Keep the same speed
exp: Reaching the point early means you are too close. Slowing slightly lets the gap grow.
src: PennDOT Driver's Manual, Managing Space, https://www.pa.gov/agencies/dmv/driver-services/pennsylvania-drivers-manual/online-drivers-manual/everyday-driving-skills/managing-space

q: Why should you leave extra room when following a motorcycle?
a: Motorcycles are always slower than cars
b: Motorcycles always take longer to stop than cars
c: Motorcycles have no brake lights
d: A motorcycle can stop quickly and its rider can fall
exp: Motorcycles can stop in less distance than cars and riders can go down suddenly, so more space gives you time to stop.
src: NHTSA Motorcycle Safety, https://www.nhtsa.gov/road-safety/motorcycles

q: Which situation calls for more following distance?
a: A dry, straight road at noon
b: A quiet street with no parked cars
c: A wet road covered with leaves
d: An empty parking lot
exp: Wet or slippery surfaces increase stopping distance, so add time to your gap.
src: PennDOT Driver's Manual, Managing Space, https://www.pa.gov/agencies/dmv/driver-services/pennsylvania-drivers-manual/online-drivers-manual/everyday-driving-skills/managing-space

q: A tailgater is behind you and you cannot change lanes. How should you adjust your space ahead?
a: Close the gap to the car ahead
b: Leave more room in front of you
c: Keep the gap exactly the same
d: Drive on the shoulder
exp: More space ahead lets you slow down gently, so the driver behind you is less likely to hit you.
src: PennDOT Driver's Manual, Managing Space, https://www.pa.gov/agencies/dmv/driver-services/pennsylvania-drivers-manual/online-drivers-manual/everyday-driving-skills/managing-space

q: What is a space cushion?
a: The padding inside your seat
b: Open room on every side of your car
c: The gap between parked cars
d: The shoulder of a highway
exp: A space cushion is open space ahead, behind and to each side that gives you time and room to react.
src: PennDOT Driver's Manual, Managing Space, https://www.pa.gov/agencies/dmv/driver-services/pennsylvania-drivers-manual/online-drivers-manual/everyday-driving-skills/managing-space

q: Parked cars are on your right and oncoming traffic is on your left, both equally close. Where should you steer?
a: Close to the parked cars
b: A middle path between the two
c: Close to the center line
d: Onto the shoulder
exp: When hazards on both sides are equal, steer between them to keep some space from each.
src: PennDOT Driver's Manual, Managing Space, https://www.pa.gov/agencies/dmv/driver-services/pennsylvania-drivers-manual/online-drivers-manual/everyday-driving-skills/managing-space

q: On a road with several lanes, why should you avoid driving right beside another car for a long time?
a: You stay in its blind spot and lose your escape path
b: It is always illegal
c: It wastes fuel
d: It makes your mirrors fog up
exp: Riding beside another car puts you in each other's blind spots and blocks a side escape. Move ahead or drop back.
src: PennDOT Driver's Manual, Managing Space, https://www.pa.gov/agencies/dmv/driver-services/pennsylvania-drivers-manual/online-drivers-manual/everyday-driving-skills/managing-space

q: Why should you leave room between your car and parked cars?
a: Parked cars may start to roll
b: It helps you parallel park
c: A door may open or a car may pull out
d: The law requires 3 feet from parked cars
exp: Doors opening and cars pulling out are common hazards along a row of parked cars.
src: PennDOT Driver's Manual, Managing Space, https://www.pa.gov/agencies/dmv/driver-services/pennsylvania-drivers-manual/online-drivers-manual/everyday-driving-skills/managing-space

q: At an intersection, why do you look left a second time before you go?
a: Traffic from the right is always faster
b: Pedestrians always cross from the left first
c: It helps you see the signal change
d: Traffic from the left reaches your path first
exp: Cars approaching from the left are in the near lane and reach you first, so check that side last.
src: State driver manuals, scanning at intersections

q: How often should you check your mirrors while driving?
a: Only when you change lanes
b: Once at the start of each trip
c: Every few seconds, and before you slow, turn or change lanes
d: About once a minute on straight roads
exp: Frequent mirror checks keep you aware of traffic around you, especially before any change in speed or position.
src: State driver manuals, scanning

q: What is a blind spot?
a: A dark stretch of road
b: A spot where parking is banned
c: A crack in the windshield
d: An area around your car you cannot see in your mirrors
exp: Blind spots are areas, mainly behind each shoulder, that your mirrors do not show.
src: PennDOT Driver's Manual, Managing Space, https://www.pa.gov/agencies/dmv/driver-services/pennsylvania-drivers-manual/online-drivers-manual/everyday-driving-skills/managing-space

q: Your car has blind spot warning lights. What does that mean for your lane changes?
a: You no longer need to check at all
b: You still need to turn your head and look
c: You can change lanes without signaling
d: You only need to check your inside mirror
exp: Sensors can miss vehicles and can be blocked by dirt or snow. They help but do not replace a head check.
src: PennDOT Driver's Manual, Managing Space, https://www.pa.gov/agencies/dmv/driver-services/pennsylvania-drivers-manual/online-drivers-manual/everyday-driving-skills/managing-space

q: How should you set your side mirrors to reduce blind spots?
a: So you can barely see the side of your own car
b: So you see mostly the side of your own car
c: Pointed at the ground
d: Pointed at the sky
exp: Turning the mirrors outward until your car just shows at the inner edge shows more of the next lane.
src: State driver manuals, mirror adjustment

q: When you pass another car on a multi-lane road, how should you move through its blind spot?
a: Slowly, staying beside it
b: Quickly, at well over the speed limit
c: By dropping back into it
d: Steadily, without lingering beside it
exp: Spending as little time as you safely can in another driver's blind spot lowers the chance they move into you.
src: PennDOT Driver's Manual, Managing Space, https://www.pa.gov/agencies/dmv/driver-services/pennsylvania-drivers-manual/online-drivers-manual/everyday-driving-skills/managing-space

q: Some freeways post a minimum speed. What should you do in heavy snow if that speed is unsafe?
a: Drive slower, stay in the right lane and leave at a safe exit if needed
b: Drive at the minimum speed no matter what
c: Drive at the minimum speed with your flashers on
d: Stay in the left lane so faster traffic can see you
exp: Safety comes first. In bad conditions you may drive below the minimum, keep right and leave the freeway if conditions stay bad.
src: State minimum speed laws; State basic speed law

q: You are about to drive down a long, steep hill. What should you do?
a: Shift to neutral and coast
b: Keep light pressure on the brake all the way down
c: Shift to a lower gear and brake firmly only when you need to slow
d: Use the parking brake to control your speed
exp: A lower gear lets the engine hold the car back, so the brakes do not overheat.
src: California Driver Handbook, https://www.dmv.ca.gov/portal/handbook/california-driver-handbook/ (Navigating the Roads); New York State Driver's Manual, Chapter 8

q: Why is riding the brakes down a long hill dangerous?
a: It makes the engine overheat
b: It drains the battery
c: It locks the wheels and causes a skid
d: The brakes can overheat and fade
exp: Brakes used all the way down a long hill can overheat and fade, and then they may not stop you.
src: California Driver Handbook, https://www.dmv.ca.gov/portal/handbook/california-driver-handbook/ (Navigating the Roads)

q: Which crash type is one of the most common for new teen drivers?
a: Running off the road, often on a curve
b: Hitting a train at a crossing
c: Backing into a parked car
d: Hitting a pedestrian at a crosswalk
exp: Run-off-road crashes, often on curves, are among the most common crashes for new teen drivers; most start with too much speed.
src: PennDOT Driver's Manual (PUB 95), Chapter 3; NHTSA teen driver data

q: You are stopped behind another car on a steep upgrade. Why should you leave extra room?
a: The car ahead may roll back when it starts
b: Your car may stall on the hill
c: Your brakes work less well uphill
d: So you can pass it when the light changes
exp: A car starting on an upgrade can roll back, so stop where you can see its rear tires.
src: PennDOT Driver's Manual, Chapter 3, Managing Space, https://www.pa.gov/agencies/dmv/driver-services/pennsylvania-drivers-manual/online-drivers-manual/everyday-driving-skills/managing-space

q: A driver behind you wants to pass. How should you adjust your space?
a: Close the gap ahead so the driver cannot cut in
b: Speed up to make the pass shorter
c: Leave more room ahead so the driver can pull back in
d: Move toward the center line
exp: Extra room ahead lets the passing driver return to the lane safely.
src: PennDOT Driver's Manual, Chapter 3, Managing Space, https://www.pa.gov/agencies/dmv/driver-services/pennsylvania-drivers-manual/online-drivers-manual/everyday-driving-skills/managing-space

q: How should you position your car as you drive through a curve?
a: Cut across the center line to straighten the curve
b: Keep to the center of your lane
c: Ride along the edge of the shoulder
d: Move as far toward the inside of the curve as you can
exp: Hold the center of your lane; drifting over the center line or onto the shoulder causes many curve crashes.
src: PennDOT Driver's Manual, Chapter 3, Managing Space, https://www.pa.gov/agencies/dmv/driver-services/pennsylvania-drivers-manual/online-drivers-manual/everyday-driving-skills/managing-space

q: On a two-lane road, when may you pass on the left?
a: When the line on your side is broken and the road ahead is clear far enough
b: Whenever the car ahead is going slower than the limit
c: When a solid yellow line is on your side
d: When the line on the other side is broken and yours is solid
exp: You may pass only with a broken line on your side, no sign forbidding it and enough clear road to finish safely.
src: New York State Driver's Manual, Chapter 6 Passing, https://dmv.ny.gov/new-york-state-drivers-manual-practice-tests/chapter-6-passing

q: In most states, within what distance of an intersection or a railroad crossing may you not pass on a two-lane road?
a: 25 feet
b: 50 feet
c: 100 feet
d: 200 feet
exp: Most states ban passing within 100 feet of an intersection, a railroad crossing, a bridge, a viaduct or a tunnel.
src: Uniform Vehicle Code (NCUTLO) 11-306; PennDOT Driver's Manual, Chapter 3, https://www.pa.gov/agencies/dmv/driver-services/pennsylvania-drivers-manual/online-drivers-manual/everyday-driving-skills/turning-merging-and-passing; New York State Driver's Manual, Chapter 6 Passing, https://dmv.ny.gov/about-dmv/chapter-6-passing

q: You are passing a car. When is it safe to return to your lane?
a: As soon as your front bumper passes its front bumper
b: When you are one car length ahead of it
c: When you can see it in your right side mirror
d: When you can see both of its headlights in your inside mirror
exp: Seeing both headlights of the passed car in your inside mirror means you have room to pull back in.
src: New York State Driver's Manual, Chapter 6 Passing, https://dmv.ny.gov/new-york-state-drivers-manual-practice-tests/chapter-6-passing

q: Another car is passing you on a two-lane road. What should you do?
a: Speed up a little so the pass is shorter
b: Move toward the center line to see ahead
c: Stay in your lane and keep a steady speed or slow slightly
d: Move onto the shoulder to give the driver room
exp: Help the passing driver get by. Never speed up while being passed.
src: New York State Driver's Manual, Chapter 6 Passing, https://dmv.ny.gov/new-york-state-drivers-manual-practice-tests/chapter-6-passing

q: What is the acceleration lane on a freeway entrance for?
a: Reaching the speed of freeway traffic before you merge
b: Stopping to wait for a gap
c: Passing slower cars on the ramp
d: Slowing down before you merge
exp: The acceleration lane gives you room to match the speed of traffic so you can merge smoothly.
src: MUTCD 11th ed., Section 3B.07; California Driver Handbook, Navigating the Roads, https://www.dmv.ca.gov/portal/handbook/california-driver-handbook/navigating-the-roads/

q: When may you pass another vehicle on the right?
a: Whenever the right shoulder is open
b: When a solid yellow line keeps you from passing on the left
c: When the vehicle ahead is turning left
d: When the vehicle ahead is going the speed limit
exp: Passing on the right is allowed when a car ahead is turning left or on roads with two or more lanes your way, never on the shoulder.
src: New York State Driver's Manual, Chapter 6 Passing, https://dmv.ny.gov/new-york-state-drivers-manual-practice-tests/chapter-6-passing

q: You just missed your freeway exit. What should you do?
a: Back up on the shoulder
b: Go on to the next exit
c: Make a U-turn through a median opening
d: Cut across the painted area to the ramp
exp: Never back up or turn around on a freeway. Take the next exit and come back.
src: State driver manuals, freeway driving

q: What is the correct order of steps for a lane change?
a: Signal, move, then check mirrors
b: Mirrors, head check, move, then signal
c: Head check, move, then signal
d: Mirrors, signal, head check, then move
exp: Check your mirrors, signal, glance over your shoulder at the blind spot, then move smoothly.
src: New York State Driver's Manual, Chapter 6 Passing, https://dmv.ny.gov/new-york-state-drivers-manual-practice-tests/chapter-6-passing

q: Your car starts to fail on a freeway. What should you do first?
a: Stop right away in your lane
b: Turn on your hazard lights and steer onto the right shoulder
c: Keep driving in your lane at normal speed until it stops
d: Pull onto the left shoulder next to the median
exp: Flashers warn others, and getting as far off the road as you can keeps you out of traffic.
src: California Driver Handbook, Navigating the Roads, https://www.dmv.ca.gov/portal/handbook/california-driver-handbook/navigating-the-roads/

q: Where should you do most of your slowing when leaving a freeway?
a: In the left lane of the freeway
b: In the travel lane before the exit
c: On the shoulder
d: In the deceleration lane or on the exit ramp
exp: Slowing in the freeway lane can cause a rear end crash. Move into the deceleration lane, then slow.
src: MUTCD 11th ed., Section 3B.07; California Driver Handbook, Navigating the Roads, https://www.dmv.ca.gov/portal/handbook/california-driver-handbook/navigating-the-roads/

q: On a road with two lanes going your way, which lane should you use for normal driving?
a: The left lane
b: The right lane
c: The left lane, once you reach the speed limit
d: The lane with the fewest cars
exp: Most states follow keep right except to pass. The left lane is for passing and left turns.
src: California Driver Handbook, Navigating the Roads, https://www.dmv.ca.gov/portal/handbook/california-driver-handbook/navigating-the-roads/

q: What is the left lane of a multi-lane highway mainly for?
a: Slow traffic
b: Entering and leaving the highway
c: Passing and getting ready to turn left
d: Parking in an emergency
exp: The left lane is used to pass or turn left. Slower traffic and entering and exiting traffic use the right lane.
src: California Driver Handbook, Navigating the Roads, https://www.dmv.ca.gov/portal/handbook/california-driver-handbook/navigating-the-roads/

q: You want to move from the far left lane to an exit on the right, three lanes over. How should you do it?
a: Change one lane at a time, checking and signaling each time
b: Cross all three lanes in one move
c: Signal once, then move across all the lanes smoothly
d: Wait until the lanes are empty, then cross in one move
exp: Moving one lane at a time lets you check each lane and lets other drivers see what you are doing.
src: California Driver Handbook, Navigating the Roads, https://www.dmv.ca.gov/portal/handbook/california-driver-handbook/navigating-the-roads/

q: On a road with three lanes your way, you want to move into the middle lane. What extra check should you make?
a: Look at the far lane, in case a car there moves into the middle too
b: Check only your inside mirror
c: Speed up first so no one can cut in
d: Check that the middle lane is moving faster
exp: A driver two lanes over may aim for the same open space at the same moment.
src: State driver manuals, changing lanes

q: What does a double solid white line between two lanes mean?
a: You may cross it freely
b: You may not cross it
c: You may cross it only to pass
d: It marks a bike lane
exp: Double solid white lane lines mark places where crossing is prohibited.
src: MUTCD 11th ed., Section 3B.06

q: The line on your side of the center line is broken, but a hill crest just ahead blocks your view. May you pass?
a: Yes, the broken line allows it
b: Yes, if you can finish before the crest
c: No, you cannot see oncoming traffic
d: Yes, if the car ahead is very slow
exp: Passing is not allowed near a curve or hill crest where you cannot see far enough ahead, whatever the line says.
src: New York State Driver's Manual, Chapter 6 Passing, https://dmv.ny.gov/new-york-state-drivers-manual-practice-tests/chapter-6-passing

q: Which of these is a place where you may not pass on a two-lane road?
a: At a railroad crossing
b: On a long straight road with a broken line
c: Where the car ahead is going 10 mph under the limit
d: Where a sign says Pass With Care
exp: Passing is banned at or near railroad crossings, intersections, bridges and tunnels.
src: New York State Driver's Manual, Chapter 6 Passing, https://dmv.ny.gov/new-york-state-drivers-manual-practice-tests/chapter-6-passing

q: While passing, what speed limit applies?
a: You may exceed the limit by 10 mph
b: There is no limit while passing
c: You must go double the other car's speed
d: You may not go over the posted limit
exp: The speed limit applies while you pass. If you cannot pass without speeding, do not pass.
src: New York State Driver's Manual, Chapter 6 Passing, https://dmv.ny.gov/new-york-state-drivers-manual-practice-tests/chapter-6-passing

q: You started to pass, but an oncoming car appears and you cannot finish in time. What should you do?
a: Speed up as fast as you can
b: Drive onto the left shoulder
c: Slow down, drop back and return to your lane behind the car
d: Finish the pass, since you are already committed
exp: Giving up on a pass is always safer than forcing it.
src: State driver manuals, passing

q: May you drive on the shoulder to pass a car on the right?
a: Yes, if you signal
b: No, unless a sign or an officer allows it
c: Yes, at low speed
d: Yes, on any freeway
exp: Drivers may not use the shoulder or edge of the road to pass unless signs or an officer direct it.
src: New York State Driver's Manual, Chapter 6 Passing, https://dmv.ny.gov/new-york-state-drivers-manual-practice-tests/chapter-6-passing

q: Many cars are passing you on the right on a multi-lane highway. What does that tell you?
a: You should speed up in the left lane
b: You should move to a lane farther right
c: The other drivers are breaking the law
d: You should stop on the shoulder
exp: If traffic keeps passing on your right, you are holding up the left lane. Move right when safe.
src: New York State Driver's Manual, Chapter 6 Passing, https://dmv.ny.gov/new-york-state-drivers-manual-practice-tests/chapter-6-passing

q: A car is passing you at night. What should you do with your headlights?
a: Switch to low beams
b: Switch to high beams
c: Keep them as they are; only the passing driver dims
d: Flash them twice
exp: Low beams keep you from blinding the passing driver as they pull alongside.
src: State driver manuals, night driving

q: As you merge onto a freeway, who usually has the right of way?
a: You, because you are merging
b: Whoever is going faster
c: Traffic already on the freeway
d: Trucks only
exp: Drivers on the freeway usually have the right of way. You must find a gap and fit in.
src: California Driver Handbook, Navigating the Roads, https://www.dmv.ca.gov/portal/handbook/california-driver-handbook/navigating-the-roads/

q: Why should you avoid stopping at the end of an acceleration lane?
a: Freeway traffic must yield to you, so a stop is never needed
b: The lane is reserved for emergency stops only
c: It is against the law to stop on any freeway ramp, even in heavy traffic
d: Joining fast traffic from a stop is very hard and dangerous
exp: From a stop you cannot reach freeway speed in time. Stop only if there is truly no gap.
src: California Driver Handbook, Navigating the Roads, https://www.dmv.ca.gov/portal/handbook/california-driver-handbook/navigating-the-roads/

q: You are driving in the right lane of a freeway and see a car on the on-ramp. What should you do?
a: Brake hard so it can merge in front of you
b: Stop in your lane
c: Move left a lane if safe, or adjust speed to let it in
d: Flash your high beams to tell it to wait
exp: Making room for merging traffic keeps the freeway flowing and prevents crashes.
src: State driver manuals, freeway driving

q: What is highway hypnosis?
a: Dizziness from motion sickness on curvy roads
b: Sleepiness caused by medicine
c: A trance from staring at oncoming headlights at night
d: A dull, half awake state from long, monotonous driving
exp: Long straight drives can lull you so you notice less. Keep your eyes moving and take breaks.
src: State driver manuals, freeway driving

q: After a long time at high speed on a freeway, why should you check your speedometer on the exit ramp?
a: The speedometer stops working at high speed
b: Lower speeds can feel slower than they really are
c: Ramps have no speed limits
d: It is required on every road test
exp: After high speed driving, a moderate speed feels like a crawl, so you may take the ramp too fast.
src: State driver manuals, freeway driving

q: What does a white diamond painted in a lane mean?
a: It is a bike lane
b: It is a bus stop
c: It marks a railroad crossing
d: It is a high occupancy vehicle (HOV) lane
exp: The diamond symbol is used only for HOV preferential lanes.
src: MUTCD 11th ed., Sections 2G.03, 2G.10 and 3E.03; California Driver Handbook, Navigating the Roads, https://www.dmv.ca.gov/portal/handbook/california-driver-handbook/navigating-the-roads/

q: A sign over a lane reads HOV 2+. Who may use the lane while the rule is in effect?
a: Vehicles carrying at least two people, counting the driver
b: Only vehicles with two or more drivers
c: Only vehicles with two axles
d: Any vehicle going over the limit
exp: The number after HOV is the minimum number of people in the vehicle, including the driver.
src: MUTCD 11th ed., Section 2G.05

q: An HOV lane is separated from the other lanes by a double solid white line. Where may you enter it?
a: Anywhere you like
b: Anywhere, if you signal
c: Only from the shoulder
d: Only where the lines are broken or signs show an opening
exp: Crossing double solid lines into or out of a special lane is not allowed. Use the marked openings.
src: California Driver Handbook, Navigating the Roads, https://www.dmv.ca.gov/portal/handbook/california-driver-handbook/navigating-the-roads/

q: Your car has broken down on the shoulder of a busy highway and it is not on fire. In most cases, what is safest?
a: Stay in the car with your seat belt on and call for help
b: Stand behind the car to wave at traffic
c: Stand in front of the car where traffic can see you
d: Walk along the shoulder to the nearest exit
exp: People standing by a disabled car are at great risk. Stay buckled in unless the car is unsafe or a safe spot away from traffic is close.
src: California Driver Handbook, Navigating the Roads, https://www.dmv.ca.gov/portal/handbook/california-driver-handbook/navigating-the-roads/

q: About how much open road ahead do you need to pass a car at 45 mph on a two-lane road?
a: About 500 feet
b: About 300 feet
c: About a quarter mile
d: About a mile
exp: At 45 mph a pass needs about a quarter mile of clear road, because it can take 10 to 20 seconds.
src: PennDOT Driver's Manual, Chapter 3, https://www.pa.gov/agencies/dmv/driver-services/pennsylvania-drivers-manual/online-drivers-manual/everyday-driving-skills/turning-merging-and-passing; Montana OPI Driver Education, Estimate Passing Gap fact sheet

q: You are on a freeway on-ramp behind a slow car. May you pass it in the acceleration lane?
a: Yes, if you signal
b: No, never use the acceleration lane to pass
c: Yes, if the freeway is empty
d: Only if the slow car waves you by
exp: The acceleration lane is for reaching freeway speed and merging, never for passing cars on the ramp.
src: PennDOT Driver's Manual, Chapter 3, https://www.pa.gov/agencies/dmv/driver-services/pennsylvania-drivers-manual/online-drivers-manual/everyday-driving-skills/turning-merging-and-passing

q: In a weave lane, some drivers are entering the freeway while others are leaving it. Who should yield?
a: Exiting drivers, because they are slowing down
b: Entering drivers, to traffic already on the freeway, including drivers exiting
c: Whoever is going slower
d: No one; both drivers keep their speed
exp: Entering drivers yield to traffic already on the freeway, including drivers moving over to exit; both take turns.
src: California Driver Handbook, https://www.dmv.ca.gov/portal/handbook/california-driver-handbook/ (Navigating the Roads); PennDOT Driver's Manual, Chapter 3, https://www.pa.gov/agencies/dmv/driver-services/pennsylvania-drivers-manual/online-drivers-manual/everyday-driving-skills/turning-merging-and-passing

q: What should you do at a truck escape ramp on a steep downgrade?
a: Use it to park and rest
b: Use it to pass slow trucks
c: Never stop in it or near its entrance
d: Stop there to check your brakes
exp: Escape ramps stop trucks whose brakes have failed; a stopped car can block one when it is needed.
src: MUTCD 11th ed., Chapter 2C (W7-4 Truck Escape Ramp signs); PennDOT Driver's Manual (PUB 95), Chapter 3

q: Why do you need a long, clear stretch of road to pass on a two-lane road?
a: A pass can take 10 to 20 seconds, and the oncoming lane must stay clear
b: The law requires a full mile of clear road for every pass
c: You must pass at least 20 mph faster than the other car
d: Passing is legal only where a passing lane is marked
exp: Even about 10 mph faster than the other car, a pass takes 10 to 20 seconds with the oncoming lane clear the whole time.
src: Montana OPI Driver Education, Estimate Passing Gap fact sheet; PennDOT Driver's Manual, Chapter 3, https://www.pa.gov/agencies/dmv/driver-services/pennsylvania-drivers-manual/online-drivers-manual/everyday-driving-skills/turning-merging-and-passing

q: You park facing uphill next to a curb. Which way should you turn your front wheels?
a: Toward the curb
b: Straight ahead
c: It does not matter if the parking brake is set
d: Away from the curb
exp: Turned away from the curb, the car rolls back and the front tire stops against the curb.
src: California Driver Handbook, Navigating the Roads (cont.), https://dmv.ca.gov/portal/handbook/california-driver-handbook/navigating-the-roads-cont1/

q: You park facing downhill next to a curb. Which way should you turn your front wheels?
a: Away from the curb
b: Toward the curb
c: Straight ahead
d: It does not matter if the parking brake is set
exp: Wheels turned toward the curb make the car roll into the curb if it moves.
src: California Driver Handbook, Navigating the Roads (cont.), https://dmv.ca.gov/portal/handbook/california-driver-handbook/navigating-the-roads-cont1/

q: You park on a hill on a road with no curb. Which way should you turn your front wheels?
a: Toward the edge of the road
b: Toward the center of the road
c: Straight ahead
d: It does not matter if the parking brake is set
exp: With no curb, turning the wheels toward the side means the car rolls off the road, not into traffic.
src: California Driver Handbook, Navigating the Roads (cont.), https://dmv.ca.gov/portal/handbook/california-driver-handbook/navigating-the-roads-cont1/

q: Which of these is a place where you may never park?
a: On a one way street, facing the direction of traffic
b: In a marked space next to a disability space
c: In a crosswalk
d: Along the curb of a quiet street with no signs
exp: Parking in a crosswalk blocks people walking and hides them from drivers. It is banned in every state.
src: California Driver Handbook, Navigating the Roads (cont.), https://dmv.ca.gov/portal/handbook/california-driver-handbook/navigating-the-roads-cont1/

q: A sign reads No Stopping. What may you do there?
a: Stop only to obey a signal or officer, or to avoid a crash
b: Stop briefly to drop off a friend
c: Stop to load packages
d: Stop for up to 3 minutes while the driver stays in the car
exp: No Stopping is the strictest of these signs. You may not stop at all except to obey traffic control or avoid a crash.
src: New York State Driver's Manual, Chapter 7, https://dmv.ny.gov/new-york-state-drivers-manual-practice-tests/chapter-7-parallel-parking

q: You are pulling away from the curb into traffic. What should you do?
a: Pull out slowly with your flashers on so others see you
b: Signal, look over your shoulder, and wait for a safe gap
c: Signal and pull out right away, since the signal gives you the right of way
d: Check your inside mirror only, then go
exp: Drivers already on the road have the right of way, so you must wait for a gap after checking your blind spot.
src: State driver manuals, parking and backing

q: How should you look when you back straight up?
a: Use only your inside mirror
b: Use only your side mirrors
c: Watch only your backup camera screen
d: Turn your body and look back through the rear window
exp: Turning to look back gives you the widest view. Mirrors alone leave large areas you cannot see.
src: State driver manuals, parking and backing

q: You drive past the driveway you wanted on a busy street. What should you do?
a: Back up in the lane to the driveway
b: Back up along the shoulder with your flashers on
c: Drive on and turn around where it is safe
d: Stop in the lane and wait for a gap to back up
exp: Do not back up in a travel lane except to parallel park; drive on and turn around safely.
src: Uniform Vehicle Code (NCUTLO) 11-1102 (limitations on backing); California Driver Handbook, https://www.dmv.ca.gov/portal/handbook/california-driver-handbook/

q: In parallel parking, where should you stop before you start backing?
a: Behind the space, in the lane
b: Halfway into the space
c: Beside the car behind the space
d: Beside the car ahead of the space, with your rear bumpers even
exp: Starting even with the car ahead, about two to three feet out, gives you the right angle to back in.
src: California Driver Handbook, Navigating the Roads (cont.), https://dmv.ca.gov/portal/handbook/california-driver-handbook/navigating-the-roads-cont1/

q: Before you open your door after parking on a street, what should you do?
a: Open it a little and wait for traffic to stop
b: Check mirrors and look over your shoulder for traffic and bikes
c: Turn on your hazard flashers, then open it
d: Open it with the hand closest to the door
exp: A door opened into traffic can hit a cyclist or be struck by a passing car.
src: California Driver Handbook, Navigating the Roads (cont.), https://dmv.ca.gov/portal/handbook/california-driver-handbook/navigating-the-roads-cont1/

q: Which steps should you take every time you park on a hill?
a: Leave the car in neutral
b: Leave the engine running
c: Shift to park, set the parking brake and turn the wheels correctly
d: Leave it in gear and skip the parking brake on a gentle hill
exp: On a hill the parking brake and the wheel position work together to keep the car from rolling into traffic.
src: California Driver Handbook, Navigating the Roads (cont.), https://dmv.ca.gov/portal/handbook/california-driver-handbook/navigating-the-roads-cont1/

q: Uphill with a curb, after turning the wheels, what do you do next?
a: Let the car roll back slowly until the front tire rests on the curb
b: Pull forward onto the curb
c: Turn the wheels straight again
d: Leave a gap of several feet from the curb
exp: Letting the tire settle against the curb lets the curb hold the car.
src: California Driver Handbook, Navigating the Roads (cont.), https://dmv.ca.gov/portal/handbook/california-driver-handbook/navigating-the-roads-cont1/

q: What does a red painted curb usually mean?
a: Loading zone only
b: Parking for a limited time
c: No stopping, standing or parking
d: Parking for people with disabilities
exp: Where curb colors are used, red means you may not stop, stand or park.
src: California Driver Handbook, Navigating the Roads (cont.), https://dmv.ca.gov/portal/handbook/california-driver-handbook/navigating-the-roads-cont1/

q: What does a blue painted curb usually mean?
a: Parking only for people with a disability placard or plate
b: Short time parking
c: Loading zone
d: No parking at any time
exp: Blue marks spaces reserved for drivers with disabilities or drivers carrying them, with a valid placard or plate.
src: California Driver Handbook, Navigating the Roads (cont.), https://dmv.ca.gov/portal/handbook/california-driver-handbook/navigating-the-roads-cont1/

q: What does a green painted curb usually mean?
a: No stopping
b: Parking for a limited time
c: Fire lane
d: Bus stop only
exp: Green allows parking for a limited time, shown on a sign or painted on the curb.
src: California Driver Handbook, Navigating the Roads (cont.), https://dmv.ca.gov/portal/handbook/california-driver-handbook/navigating-the-roads-cont1/

q: What does a white painted curb usually mean?
a: Park all day
b: No stopping at any time
c: Disability parking
d: Stop only long enough to pick up or drop off people
exp: White allows a short stop to load or unload passengers or mail.
src: California Driver Handbook, Navigating the Roads (cont.), https://dmv.ca.gov/portal/handbook/california-driver-handbook/navigating-the-roads-cont1/

q: What does a yellow painted curb usually mean?
a: Parking for people with disabilities
b: Park as long as you like
c: Loading zone; stop only to load or unload
d: Bike parking only
exp: Yellow marks a loading zone with a time limit.
src: California Driver Handbook, Navigating the Roads (cont.), https://dmv.ca.gov/portal/handbook/california-driver-handbook/navigating-the-roads-cont1/

q: What does double parking mean?
a: Parking on the street side of a car already parked at the curb
b: Parking across two spaces in a lot
c: Parking with two wheels on the curb
d: Parking two cars in one driveway
exp: A double parked car blocks a traffic lane and is not allowed.
src: California Driver Handbook, Navigating the Roads (cont.), https://dmv.ca.gov/portal/handbook/california-driver-handbook/navigating-the-roads-cont1/

q: Which of these is never a legal place to park?
a: In a marked space in a parking garage
b: Beside a curb with no signs
c: In a marked parallel space
d: Right next to a fire hydrant
exp: A car beside a hydrant blocks firefighters. The exact distance comes from state law.
src: California Driver Handbook, Navigating the Roads (cont.), https://dmv.ca.gov/portal/handbook/california-driver-handbook/navigating-the-roads-cont1/

q: May you park in the striped area next to a disability parking space?
a: Yes, if you have a small car
b: Yes, for up to 15 minutes
c: No, that area is needed for wheelchairs and ramps
d: Yes, if you stay in the car
exp: The striped access aisle must stay clear so a person can get in and out of a vehicle.
src: California Driver Handbook, Navigating the Roads (cont.), https://dmv.ca.gov/portal/handbook/california-driver-handbook/navigating-the-roads-cont1/

q: Which sign still allows you to stop briefly to load or unload things?
a: No Stopping
b: No Parking
c: No Standing
d: Tow-Away Zone
exp: A No Parking sign still lets you stop while you load or unload people or things. No Standing allows only picking up or dropping off people, and No Stopping allows neither.
src: New York State Driver's Manual, Chapter 7, https://dmv.ny.gov/new-york-state-drivers-manual-practice-tests/chapter-7-parallel-parking

q: While backing into a parallel space, at about what angle should your car be before you straighten the wheel?
a: About 10 degrees
b: About 45 degrees
c: About 90 degrees
d: Straight in line with the curb
exp: Back to about a 45 degree angle, then straighten, then turn the other way to swing in.
src: California Driver Handbook, Navigating the Roads (cont.), https://dmv.ca.gov/portal/handbook/california-driver-handbook/navigating-the-roads-cont1/

q: How long should a parallel parking space be?
a: Several feet longer than your car
b: Exactly the length of your car
c: About the same length as your car
d: At least twice as long as your car
exp: You need extra room in front and behind to swing the car into the space.
src: California Driver Handbook, Navigating the Roads (cont.), https://dmv.ca.gov/portal/handbook/california-driver-handbook/navigating-the-roads-cont1/

q: Your first parallel parking try goes badly. What is the best choice?
a: Keep turning back and forth in the space until it fits
b: Leave it far from the curb
c: Pull out and start again
d: Bump gently against the car behind to line up
exp: A clean second try is better than many small corrections or hitting the curb.
src: State driver manuals, parking and backing

q: What should you do before you leave your parked car?
a: Leave the engine running
b: Leave a child in the car for a minute
c: Shift to neutral
d: Set the parking brake and take the key with you
exp: Setting the brake and taking the key keeps the car from rolling or being driven off.
src: California Driver Handbook, Navigating the Roads (cont.), https://dmv.ca.gov/portal/handbook/california-driver-handbook/navigating-the-roads-cont1/

q: You want the back of your car to go right while backing. Which way do you turn the wheel?
a: To the left
b: Keep it straight
c: To the right
d: Turn it all the way left, then right
exp: When backing, turn the wheel in the direction you want the rear of the car to go.
src: State driver manuals, parking and backing

q: How fast should you back up?
a: At the posted speed limit
b: Quickly, to spend less time in reverse
c: At the same speed you drive forward
d: Slowly, at about walking speed or less
exp: Low speed gives you time to stop for anything you did not see behind the car.
src: State driver manuals, parking and backing

q: Your car has a backup camera. How should you use it?
a: As your only check
b: As a helper, along with mirrors and looking over your shoulder
c: Only at night
d: Only on the road test
exp: Cameras do not show everything and can be blocked. Look back yourself as well.
src: State driver manuals, parking and backing

q: You are backing out of a driveway onto a street. Where should you stop first to look?
a: At the sidewalk, to check for people walking
b: In the middle of the street
c: Only at the far curb
d: You should not stop at all
exp: Stopping at the sidewalk lets you check for people before you look for street traffic.
src: State driver manuals, parking and backing

q: Why should you look over your shoulder before pulling out from a parallel space?
a: To check that your rear bumper clears the car behind
b: To check your rear tire
c: To read signs behind you
d: A car or bike may be hidden in your blind spot
exp: Your mirrors do not show the blind spot beside and behind you, where a car or cyclist may be coming.
src: State driver manuals, parking and backing

q: You are driving out of an alley onto a street. What should you do before crossing the sidewalk?
a: Stop and yield to people walking
b: Honk and keep going
c: Speed up to clear the sidewalk
d: Flash your lights and enter
exp: Most states require a stop before the sidewalk when leaving an alley or driveway, then you yield to traffic.
src: State driver manuals, parking and backing

q: When may you back up in a travel lane?
a: Whenever traffic is light
b: Only to parallel park
c: When your hazard flashers are on and traffic is light
d: To reach a driveway you just passed
exp: Backing in a travel lane surprises other drivers; do it only to parallel park.
src: Uniform Vehicle Code (NCUTLO) 11-1102; California Driver Handbook, https://www.dmv.ca.gov/portal/handbook/california-driver-handbook/

q: You are stopped at an intersection with no painted crosswalk lines. A person on the corner starts to cross in front of you. What should you do?
a: Go ahead, because only painted lines give a pedestrian the right of way
b: Yield, because the corner is an unmarked crosswalk
c: Yield only if a WALK signal is showing
d: Go if your light is green, since the person must wait
exp: At an intersection the place where the sidewalk would continue is an unmarked crosswalk, and you must yield to pedestrians in it.
src: State driver manuals, pedestrian right of way; NHTSA pedestrian safety

q: The car in the lane next to you stops just before a crosswalk for no reason you can see. What should you do?
a: Keep going, since your own lane is clear
b: Slow down and pass it carefully
c: Change lanes behind it, then pass
d: Slow down and stop, because someone may be crossing in front of it
exp: A stopped car can hide a pedestrian from you. Never pass a vehicle stopped at a crosswalk.
src: NHTSA, Pedestrian Safety, tips for drivers

q: A pedestrian is crossing with a white cane. Your light turns green. What should you do?
a: Stay stopped until the person has finished crossing
b: Go, since your green light gives you the right of way
c: Tap your horn lightly so the person knows where you are
d: Creep forward slowly so the person knows you are waiting
exp: White cane laws in every state require drivers to yield to a blind pedestrian, even on a green light.
src: National Federation of the Blind, Braille Monitor, April 2025 (white cane laws in all 50 states); American Council of the Blind state white cane law compilation, acb.org/whitecane

q: You come up behind a cyclist on a two lane road and oncoming traffic is close. What should you do?
a: Pass now, staying just inside your own lane
b: Stay behind the cyclist until you can pass with a wide gap
c: Cross partly into the oncoming lane and pass quickly
d: Follow closely so you can pass the moment traffic clears
exp: Wait until you can leave at least the distance your state requires (see the box in 9.2), and more at higher speeds. Passing too close can knock a rider down.
src: NHTSA, Bicycle Safety; NCSL, Safely Passing Bicyclists chart

q: A motorcycle is riding near the left edge of its lane. May you drive beside it in the same lane?
a: Yes, if the rider stays near one edge and there is room
b: Yes, but only in slow traffic
c: Yes, if you stay at least 3 feet from the rider
d: No, a motorcycle is entitled to the full lane
exp: A motorcycle has the right to the full width of a lane. Never share a lane with one.
src: State driver manuals, sharing the road with motorcycles

q: You are driving next to a large truck. How can you tell if the truck driver can see you?
a: If you can see the driver's face in the truck's side mirror
b: If you are right beside the cab
c: If you are close behind the trailer
d: If you can see the truck's turn signals
exp: If you cannot see the driver in the truck's side mirror, the driver cannot see you.
src: FMCSA, Tips for Driving Safely Around Large Trucks or Buses

q: A truck ahead of you is signaling a right turn but moves to the left first. What should you do?
a: Pass it on the right while it waits
b: Pull up beside it so the driver can see you
c: Stay back and do not move into the space between the truck and the curb
d: Move into the gap by the curb and turn first
exp: Trucks swing wide to turn right. The gap on the right closes as the trailer turns.
src: FMCSA, Tips for Driving Safely Around Large Trucks or Buses

q: You see a fluorescent orange triangle with a red border on the back of a tractor. What does it mean?
a: The vehicle is carrying hazardous materials
b: The vehicle is built to travel at about 25 mph or less
c: The vehicle is about to turn left
d: You may never pass it
exp: That is the slow moving vehicle emblem. Slow down at once, because you will close the gap quickly.
src: Ohio State University Ag Safety, SMV emblem; ASABE S276

q: A deer suddenly appears in your lane and you cannot stop in time. What is the safest action?
a: Swerve hard onto the shoulder
b: Swerve into the oncoming lane
c: Steer sharply around it, then brake
d: Brake firmly and stay in your lane
exp: Swerving can send you into oncoming traffic, a tree or a ditch, which is often worse than hitting the animal.
src: Missouri Driver Guide, Chapter 8 (animals); state driver manuals, animals

q: You come up behind a horse-drawn buggy on a rural road. What should you do?
a: Tap your horn early so the driver knows you are there
b: Pass quickly to spend less time near the horse
c: Slow down well before reaching it and pass slowly with plenty of room
d: Pass as you would a car, then pull right back in
exp: Sudden noise can spook a horse. Slow down, do not honk or rev the engine, and pass with a wide gap.
src: State driver manuals, horses and horse-drawn vehicles

q: Why should you not honk at a blind pedestrian who is waiting to cross?
a: The person uses traffic sounds to judge when to cross
b: Honking is only illegal near schools
c: It tells the person that it is safe to cross
d: The person cannot hear a horn
exp: A blind pedestrian listens to traffic to decide when it is safe, and a horn can confuse or startle them.
src: State white cane laws; state driver manuals, pedestrians

q: Where should you stop for a pedestrian at a marked crosswalk?
a: On the crosswalk lines
b: Just short of the person, so they know you see them
c: Before the crosswalk, far enough back that other drivers can see the person
d: Past the crosswalk, out of the way
exp: Stop before the crosswalk and far enough back that drivers in other lanes can see the pedestrian too.
src: NHTSA, Pedestrian Safety, tips for drivers

q: You are turning right on a green light. What must you check for before you start the turn?
a: Only cars behind you
b: Only vehicles coming from your right
c: Traffic signals on the cross street
d: Pedestrians crossing the street you are turning into
exp: People crossing the street you turn into often have a WALK signal at the same time as your green light.
src: State driver manuals, turning and pedestrians

q: What is the safest habit before backing out of a driveway where children live?
a: Back quickly so you spend less time in the street
b: Walk around the car before getting in, then back slowly
c: Honk twice and then back out
d: Rely on your rearview mirror alone
exp: Small children can be below the line of your rear window. Check behind the car first and back slowly.
src: NHTSA, Pedestrian Safety; state driver manuals, backing

q: On a public road, a person riding a bicycle has:
a: Fewer rights than drivers, because a bike is not a vehicle
b: The right to ignore stop signs
c: The same rights and duties as the driver of a vehicle
d: No duty to signal turns
exp: Cyclists on the road must obey the same traffic laws as drivers and have the same rights.
src: State vehicle codes; NHTSA, Bicycle Safety

q: A cyclist is riding near the middle of a narrow lane. Why might the rider do this?
a: To stop drivers from squeezing past where there is not enough room
b: Because the law requires cyclists to ride in the center of every lane
c: To slow down traffic on purpose
d: Because the rider is about to turn right
exp: Cyclists may move left to avoid hazards or to keep drivers from passing too closely in a narrow lane.
src: State driver manuals, sharing the road with bicycles

q: What is a right hook crash?
a: A cyclist turning left in front of a car
b: A car rear ending a cyclist at a light
c: A driver passing a cyclist and then turning right across the cyclist's path
d: A car door opening into a cyclist
exp: Before turning right, check your mirror and over your shoulder for a bike beside you, and let it go first.
src: NHTSA, Bicycle Safety, right turns

q: What does a sharrow painted in a traffic lane tell you?
a: Bicycles are not allowed in that lane
b: Cars may not use that lane
c: The lane is for buses only
d: Expect cyclists to share that lane
exp: A sharrow, a bicycle symbol with two arrowheads, marks a lane shared by cars and bikes.
src: MUTCD 11th ed., Section 9E.09 (shared lane marking)

q: You park on a busy street with a bike lane beside you. What should you do before opening your door?
a: Open it quickly so you block traffic for less time
b: Check your side mirror and look back over your shoulder
c: Open it only a few inches, then all the way
d: Honk to warn cyclists
exp: A door opened into a cyclist's path can throw the rider into traffic. Look for bikes first.
src: State driver manuals, sharing the road with bicycles

q: When may you drive in a marked bike lane?
a: To cross it to reach a driveway or parking space, after yielding to cyclists
b: Never, under any condition
c: Whenever traffic in your lane is slow
d: When you want to pass a car on the right
exp: You may cross a bike lane to turn or park, but you must yield to cyclists and must not drive along it.
src: State driver manuals, bike lanes; MUTCD 11th ed., Chapter 9E

q: You want to turn left and a motorcycle is coming toward you. What should you assume?
a: It is farther away than it looks
b: It will stop for you
c: It is closer and moving faster than it looks
d: It is slowing to turn
exp: A motorcycle's small size makes it look farther away and slower than it is, a common cause of left turn crashes.
src: NHTSA, Motorcycle Safety; state driver manuals

q: Why should you leave extra following distance behind a motorcycle?
a: Riders often change lanes without signaling
b: Motorcycles always ride slower than the limit
c: It is required only at night
d: A rider may slow down without a brake light coming on, and motorcycles can stop quickly
exp: Riders often slow by easing off the throttle or downshifting, which does not light the brake light.
src: State driver manuals, sharing the road with motorcycles

q: A motorcycle ahead has had its turn signal flashing for a long time. What should you do?
a: Pull out in front of it, since it is turning
b: Wait until you are sure it is really turning
c: Flash your high beams at it
d: Pass it in the same lane
exp: Many motorcycle signals do not cancel by themselves, so a flashing signal may have been left on.
src: State driver manuals, sharing the road with motorcycles

q: Which side of a large truck has the largest blind spot?
a: The right side
b: The left side
c: The front
d: The rear
exp: The no-zone along the right side can cover more than one lane and most of the trailer's length.
src: FMCSA, Tips for Driving Safely Around Large Trucks or Buses; NY GTSC truck safety tips

q: After passing a truck, when is it safe to move back in front of it?
a: As soon as your rear bumper clears its cab
b: When the truck flashes its lights
c: When you can see the whole front of the truck in your rearview mirror
d: When you are one car length ahead
exp: Wait until you can see the truck's front in your inside mirror, then move over without slowing down.
src: FMCSA, Tips for Driving Safely Around Large Trucks or Buses

q: Why is it dangerous to cut in close in front of a large truck and then slow down?
a: Trucks must keep a set speed on highways
b: Truck drivers sit too low to see you
c: Truck brakes work well only at low speed
d: A truck needs far more distance than a car to stop
exp: A large truck at highway speed can need close to the length of two football fields to stop.
src: FMCSA, Tips for Driving Safely Around Large Trucks or Buses

q: Why should you avoid passing a truck on a long downhill grade?
a: Trucks have more blind spots on hills
b: Trucks tend to pick up speed going downhill
c: Passing is illegal on any hill
d: Trucks always slow down sharply on hills
exp: Large vehicles gain speed going down hills, so the gap you need to pass can close quickly.
src: FMCSA, Tips for Driving Safely Around Large Trucks or Buses

q: A city bus at a stop signals that it is pulling back into traffic. What is the best choice?
a: Slow down and let it pull out
b: Speed up to get ahead of it
c: Pass it on the right
d: Flash your lights to tell the driver to wait
exp: Letting a bus back into traffic is the safe choice. Buses also have no-zones and make wide turns, like trucks.
src: State driver manuals, sharing the road with buses

q: A slow tractor ahead is slowing down near a farm gate on the left. What should you do?
a: Pass it on the left before it turns
b: Pass it on the shoulder
c: Sound your horn and pass
d: Do not pass, because it may be about to turn left
exp: Farm vehicles often turn into fields and driveways and may have no visible turn signals.
src: State driver manuals, slow moving vehicles

q: One deer crosses the road ahead of you at dusk. What should you expect?
a: The road is now clear
b: More deer may follow it
c: The deer will run away from your headlights
d: Deer cross only one at a time
exp: Deer usually travel in groups, so slow down and watch for others after one crosses.
src: State driver manuals, animals; Missouri Driver Guide, Chapter 8

q: You see a yellow diamond sign with a bicycle and a SHARE THE ROAD plaque below it. What does it mean?
a: Bicycles must ride on the shoulder here
b: Cyclists may use the lane with you, so slow down and give them room
c: A bike lane starts ahead and cars may not enter it
d: Bicycles are not allowed on this road
exp: The older SHARE THE ROAD plaque, still seen on many roads, tells you that the vehicle shown on the sign above it uses the lane with you.
src: MUTCD 2009 ed. W16-1P SHARE THE ROAD plaque (dropped from the 11th ed.; existing signs remain); state manuals

q: You are stopped behind a horse-drawn buggy at the bottom of a hill. Why should you leave extra space?
a: You will need room to pass it on the hill
b: The buggy driver will pull over at the bottom to let you pass
c: Horses often stop to rest at the foot of a hill
d: The buggy can roll back as it starts up the hill
exp: A buggy has no engine to hold it on a slope, so it can roll back as the horse starts to pull.
src: PennDOT Driver's Manual (PUB 95), sharing the road with horse-drawn vehicles; state driver manuals

q: A car in the next lane has stopped at a crosswalk to let a pedestrian cross. When may you pass it?
a: When the pedestrian is not yet in your lane
b: When you slow to about 10 mph
c: Not until the car moves on and the crosswalk is clear
d: When you have checked your blind spot
exp: The stopped car may hide a person crossing in front of it. Never pass a vehicle stopped for a pedestrian.
src: Uniform Vehicle Code 11-504(d); NHTSA, Pedestrian Safety, tips for drivers

q: An oncoming car is approaching at night and you have your high beams on. What should you do?
a: Keep high beams on until the other driver dims theirs
b: Switch to parking lights until it passes
c: Switch to low beams well before it gets close
d: Switch to low beams once it has passed you
exp: Low beams keep from blinding the other driver. Most states set exact distances; see the box in Chapter 10.
src: State driver manuals, headlight use; state headlight laws

q: Your car has antilock brakes and you must stop fast. What should you do?
a: Pump the brake pedal quickly
b: Press lightly and steer around the hazard
c: Press hard, release when the pedal pulses, then press again
d: Press hard, keep pressing and steer if needed
exp: With ABS, press firmly and hold. The pulsing you feel is normal, and you can still steer.
src: Missouri Driver Guide, Chapter 9 (ABS: do not pump, keep your foot on the brake, steer)

q: The rear of your car starts to slide to the right. What should you do?
a: Ease off the gas and steer gently to the right, where you want to go
b: Brake hard and hold the pedal down
c: Steer hard to the left
d: Ease off the gas and steer to the left
exp: Take your foot off the gas, look where you want to go and steer gently that way.
src: Missouri Driver Guide, Chapter 9 (skids)

q: Your steering suddenly feels light on a road covered with water. What is happening, and what should you do?
a: The tires are hydroplaning; brake hard
b: The power steering failed; turn off the engine
c: The tires are hydroplaning; steer sharply toward the shoulder
d: The tires are hydroplaning; ease off the gas and do not brake hard
exp: In hydroplaning the tires ride on water. Ease off the gas and hold the wheel steady until they grip again.
src: Missouri Driver Guide, Chapter 9 (hydroplaning)

q: Your accelerator sticks and the car keeps speeding up. What should you do first?
a: Turn off the engine right away
b: Look down and pull the pedal up with your hand
c: Shift to neutral, then brake and steer off the road
d: Pull the parking brake hard
exp: Neutral cuts power to the wheels while keeping power steering and brakes working.
src: Missouri Driver Guide, Chapter 9 (stuck accelerator)

q: Police lights flash behind you and you pull over. What should you do next?
a: Get out and walk back to the patrol car
b: Stay in the car with your hands on the wheel and wait for the officer
c: Find your license in the glove box right away so you are ready
d: Turn off every light inside the car, even at night
exp: Stay in the car with your hands where the officer can see them, and reach for documents only when asked.
src: State driver manuals, traffic stops (for example PennDOT PUB 95; New York DMV Driver's Manual, Chapter 1)

q: You are in a minor crash. No one is hurt and both cars can be driven. What should you usually do?
a: Move the cars out of the travel lanes, then exchange information
b: Leave the cars where they stopped until the police arrive
c: Exchange information standing between the cars in the lane
d: Leave if the other driver agrees
exp: If no one is hurt and the cars can be driven, moving them out of traffic prevents a second crash. You must still stop and exchange information.
src: FHWA, Traffic Incident Management Quick Clearance Laws

q: When is a road usually most slippery in the rain?
a: During the first few minutes of rain after a dry spell
b: After several hours of heavy rain
c: Right after the rain stops
d: When the rain is heaviest
exp: Oil and dirt on the pavement mix with the first rain into a slick film.
src: Missouri Driver Guide, Chapter 9; state driver manuals, wet roads

q: Which lights should you use when driving in fog?
a: High beams
b: Your hazard flashers instead of headlights
c: Low beams
d: Parking lights only
exp: High beams reflect off fog back into your eyes. Low beams light the road without the glare.
src: Missouri Driver Guide, Chapter 9 (fog)

q: Your brake pedal suddenly sinks to the floor. What should you try first?
a: Turn off the engine
b: Pump the brake pedal fast and hard
c: Pull the parking brake as hard as you can
d: Shift into park
exp: Pumping may build up enough pressure to stop. If not, use the parking brake slowly and shift to a lower gear.
src: Missouri Driver Guide, Chapter 9 (brake failure)

q: You are following another car at night on a dark road. Which lights should you use?
a: High beams, so you can see past the car
b: Low beams, so you do not glare in its mirrors
c: Parking lights only
d: Fog lights only
exp: Your high beams shine into the other driver's mirrors and blind them, so use low beams when following.
src: State driver manuals, headlight use; distance varies by state

q: An oncoming driver will not dim their high beams. Where should you look?
a: Straight into the headlights
b: At the center line
c: At your dashboard
d: Toward the right edge line of your lane
exp: Looking down and to the right at the edge line keeps you in your lane without staring into the glare.
src: State driver manuals, night driving

q: What does it mean to overdrive your headlights?
a: Driving so fast that you cannot stop within the distance your lights show
b: Using high beams in town
c: Driving with only one working headlight
d: Leaving your lights on after you park
exp: If you cannot stop within the reach of your headlights, you will not be able to stop for something that appears there.
src: Missouri Driver Guide, Chapter 9; state driver manuals, night driving

q: Which is true about headlight use?
a: Headlights are needed only after full dark
b: Daytime running lights count as headlights at dusk
c: Daytime running lights are not enough, because they may leave your taillights off
d: Using low beams in daytime rain is illegal
exp: Daytime running lights often light only the front of the car. Use your headlights at night and whenever it is hard to see.
src: Uniform Vehicle Code 12-201; state driver manuals, headlight use

q: How can you reduce glare from headlights behind you at night?
a: Turn on your dome light
b: Flip the day and night tab on your inside mirror
c: Tap your brakes
d: Tilt your side mirrors down
exp: The night setting on the inside mirror dims the reflected glare from vehicles behind you.
src: State driver manuals, night driving

q: Hydroplaning can start at speeds as low as about:
a: 15 mph
b: 65 mph
c: 80 mph
d: 35 mph
exp: Hydroplaning can begin around 35 mph, and the risk rises with speed, worn tread and low tire pressure.
src: Missouri Driver Guide, Chapter 9 (hydroplaning)

q: Why should you not use cruise control on a wet road?
a: It can keep feeding power to the wheels if the car starts to slide
b: It uses more fuel in rain
c: It turns off your headlights
d: It is illegal in every state
exp: If the tires lose grip, cruise control may keep the wheels driving and make the skid worse.
src: Missouri Driver Guide, Chapter 9

q: Water is flowing across the road ahead and you cannot see the pavement. What should you do?
a: Drive through slowly in low gear
b: Turn around and find another route
c: Drive through quickly to avoid stalling
d: Follow another car through
exp: About a foot of moving water can carry away most cars, and the road under it may be washed out.
src: National Weather Service, Turn Around Don't Drown

q: After driving slowly through deep water, what should you do?
a: Brake hard once to test the brakes
b: Shift to neutral
c: Press the brakes lightly a few times to dry them
d: Turn off the engine to cool it
exp: Wet brakes may not work well. Light pressure while driving slowly dries them.
src: State driver manuals, wet brakes

q: The fog becomes so thick that you cannot see well enough to drive. What should you do?
a: Stop in your lane with your hazard flashers on
b: Pull as far off the road as you can, turn on your hazard flashers and wait
c: Follow the taillights of the car ahead
d: Switch to high beams and continue
exp: Stopping in a travel lane invites a rear end crash. Get fully off the road and wait for the fog to lift.
src: Missouri Driver Guide, Chapter 9 (fog)

q: In fog, why should you avoid steering by the taillights of the car ahead?
a: It is illegal
b: Taillights do not show in fog
c: It wastes fuel
d: If that car leaves the road or stops, you may follow it
exp: The right edge line is a safer guide than another driver who may be lost or about to stop.
src: State driver manuals, fog

q: In freezing weather, which part of the road is likely to freeze first?
a: Bridges and overpasses
b: Flat roads in open country
c: A road through a town
d: A road with heavy traffic
exp: Cold air passes over and under bridges, so they freeze before the rest of the road.
src: Missouri Driver Guide, Chapter 9 (snow and ice)

q: What is black ice?
a: Ice mixed with dirt
b: Snow that has turned gray
c: A thin clear layer of ice that looks like wet pavement
d: Ice that forms only at night in cities
exp: Black ice is hard to see. If the road looks wet but there is no spray from tires ahead, suspect ice.
src: State driver manuals, winter driving

q: Your car has four-wheel drive. How does it help on an icy road?
a: It lets you stop in half the distance
b: It helps you get moving but does not help you stop
c: It lets you drive at the normal speed limit
d: It prevents all skids
exp: Four-wheel and all-wheel drive help with traction when starting, not with braking or turning on ice.
src: Missouri Driver Guide, Chapter 9 (snow and ice)

q: Compared with a dry road, how much distance can you need to stop on ice?
a: About the same, if your car has ABS
b: About twice as much
c: About half as much again
d: Up to about ten times as much
exp: On ice, stopping can take up to about ten times the distance it takes on dry pavement, so leave a far larger gap and slow to a crawl.
src: PennDOT Driver's Manual (PUB 95), Chapter 3, adverse conditions (ice: about ten times the space); state driver manuals, winter driving

q: In a hard stop without antilock brakes, what should you do if the wheels lock?
a: Ease off the pedal a little, then press again
b: Keep pressing harder
c: Pull the parking brake
d: Turn the steering wheel sharply
exp: A car with locked wheels cannot be steered. Releasing slightly lets the wheels turn again.
src: State driver manuals, braking

q: A front tire blows out at highway speed. What should you do first?
a: Brake hard right away
b: Steer hard toward the shoulder
c: Hold the wheel firmly and ease off the gas
d: Shift to neutral and turn off the engine
exp: Keep the car straight and let it slow down before braking gently and pulling off the road.
src: Missouri Driver Guide, Chapter 9 (tire blowout)

q: Your right wheels drop off the pavement onto the shoulder. What should you do?
a: Jerk the wheel left to get back on fast
b: Ease off the gas, keep going straight, and return gently when it is safe
c: Brake hard on the shoulder
d: Speed up to climb back onto the road
exp: Jerking the wheel can throw the car across the road. Slow down and steer back gently.
src: Missouri Driver Guide, Chapter 9 (off road recovery)

q: You see smoke coming from under your hood. After pulling over and turning off the engine, what should you do?
a: Open the hood to look for the fire
b: Pour water on the engine
c: Drive slowly to the nearest service station
d: Get everyone out and away from the car, then call 911
exp: Opening the hood lets in fresh air that can feed a fire. Move well away and call for help.
src: Texas Department of Insurance, Car Fire Safety (stay at least 100 feet away, do not open the hood); state driver manuals, vehicle fire

q: Which information should drivers exchange after a crash?
a: Names, license numbers, plate numbers and insurance information
b: Only phone numbers
c: Only insurance company names
d: Only driver license numbers
exp: Drivers exchange names, addresses, license and plate numbers and insurance details.
src: State driver manuals, crash procedures

q: You back into a parked car and no one is around. What must you do?
a: Leave, since no one saw it
b: Wait one minute, then leave
c: Leave a note with your name and contact information, and report it as your state requires
d: Call your insurance company only
exp: Leaving without giving your information is a hit and run. Leave a note and report it.
src: State driver manuals, crash with unattended vehicle

q: Where should your hands be on the steering wheel?
a: At about 9 and 3 or 8 and 4 o'clock
b: Both hands together at the top of the wheel
c: One hand at the bottom of the wheel
d: Anywhere that feels comfortable, as long as one hand is on the wheel
exp: From 9 and 3 or 8 and 4 you can steer quickly, and your arms stay clear of the airbag.
src: PennDOT Driver's Manual (PUB 95), Chapter 3, special circumstances and emergencies; NHTSA, Using Efficient Steering Techniques

q: You are driving at 45 mph when a box falls into your lane close ahead, and the lane beside you is clear. What is often the better choice?
a: Lock the brakes so the car stops as fast as it can
b: Steer around it into the clear lane
c: Brake hard and keep the wheel straight
d: Swerve sharply into the nearest lane without looking
exp: Above about 25 mph, steering around a hazard often takes less distance than stopping. Check that the escape path is clear.
src: PennDOT Driver's Manual (PUB 95), Chapter 3, special circumstances and emergencies

q: A car is coming toward you in your lane. What should you do?
a: Swerve left into the oncoming lane
b: Stop in your lane and wait
c: Flash your lights and hold your speed
d: Sound your horn, slow down and steer to the right
exp: Steering right takes you away from the other car. Swerving left fails if the other driver swings back into their own lane.
src: PennDOT Driver's Manual (PUB 95), Chapter 3, special circumstances and emergencies

q: Your car breaks down on a two-lane road. What should you do first?
a: Get it as far off the road as you can and turn on your hazard flashers
b: Leave it in the lane and walk for help
c: Stand behind the car and wave traffic around it
d: Raise the hood while the car is still in the lane
exp: Get the car out of traffic and turn on the flashers. Raise the hood only if you can do it without stepping into traffic.
src: State driver manuals, vehicle breakdowns

q: A police officer stops you at night. What should you do inside the car?
a: Turn off all lights so you do not blind the officer
b: Turn on the interior light and keep your hands on the wheel
c: Get your papers out of the glove box before the officer arrives
d: Step out and meet the officer halfway
exp: An interior light and hands on the wheel let the officer see that you are not a threat.
src: State driver manuals, traffic stops (for example PennDOT PUB 95)

q: Police lights flash behind you on a road with no shoulder. What should you do?
a: Stop right away in your lane
b: Speed up to find a place to stop
c: Pull to the left side of the road
d: Signal and drive slowly to the nearest safe spot on the right
exp: Pull over to the right as soon as it is safe. If there is no safe spot, keep driving slowly to the nearest one.
src: State driver manuals, traffic stops

q: In a car without ABS, what is threshold braking?
a: Pressing firmly to just short of locking the wheels
b: Pressing the pedal as hard as you can and holding it
c: Using only the parking brake
d: Shifting to neutral before you brake
exp: Braking just short of lockup stops you fast while the wheels keep rolling, so you can still steer.
src: State driver manuals, braking (threshold braking)

q: Your wheels start to spin as you pull away on snow. What should you do?
a: Press the gas harder
b: Turn the wheel back and forth quickly
c: Ease off the gas
d: Shift to neutral
exp: Spinning wheels have lost grip. Easing off the gas lets the tires grip again.
src: State driver manuals, winter driving

q: An oncoming driver keeps high beams on as you approach at night. What should you do first?
a: Flash your high beams once, quickly
b: Turn on your high beams and leave them on until the driver dims
c: Look straight at the lights to judge the distance
d: Stop in your lane until the car passes
exp: A quick flash reminds the other driver to dim. If the glare stays, look down and to the right at the edge line and slow down.
src: PennDOT Driver's Manual (PUB 95), Chapter 3 (night driving); New York State Driver's Manual, Chapter 9

q: It starts to rain. How should you change your following distance?
a: Keep it the same as long as you slow down
b: Shorten it so other cars do not cut in
c: Add at least 2 seconds, and more in heavy rain
d: Add one car length
exp: Wet roads take longer to stop on. Add at least 2 seconds to your normal gap, more in heavy rain.
src: PennDOT Driver's Manual (PUB 95), Chapter 3 (following distance); NHTSA and state driver manuals, wet weather

q: You are about to drive on a snowy morning. What should you do first?
a: Clear a small spot on the windshield and go
b: Warm up the engine so the defroster works, then clear the windows, lights and roof
c: Leave the snow on the roof, since it will blow off
d: Drive off at once and let the heater clear the glass
exp: A warm engine lets the defroster clear the glass. Snow left on the roof can slide over your windshield or hit the car behind.
src: PennDOT Driver's Manual (PUB 95), Chapter 3 (winter driving)

q: You are driving on packed snow. What is a common guide for your speed?
a: The posted limit, if you have snow tires
b: About 5 mph below normal
c: Your normal speed with your flashers on
d: About half your normal speed
exp: Packed snow gives far less grip than dry pavement. Slowing to about half your normal speed is a common guide.
src: PennDOT Driver's Manual (PUB 95), Chapter 3 (winter driving)

q: You have had three beers at a party and need to drive in 30 minutes. What will lower your blood alcohol concentration?
a: Drinking two cups of black coffee
b: Only time
c: Taking a cold shower
d: Eating a large meal now
exp: Your liver clears alcohol at a slow, steady rate. Coffee, showers and food after drinking do not lower BAC.
src: NIAAA; state driver manuals, alcohol section

q: For a driver 21 or older, what blood alcohol concentration makes driving illegal even if the driving looks normal?
a: 0.10 or higher
b: 0.12 or higher
c: 0.15 or higher
d: 0.08 or higher
exp: At 0.08 or higher, a driver 21 or older is over the legal limit. Below it, you can still be charged if alcohol affects your driving.
src: https://www.nhtsa.gov/risky-driving/drunk-driving

q: What is a zero tolerance law?
a: A ban on alcohol in every car
b: A rule that all drivers must take a breath test
c: A very low BAC limit for drivers under 21
d: A law that sets the adult limit at zero
exp: Every state has a zero tolerance law that sets a far lower BAC limit for drivers under 21, low enough that one drink can break it.
src: 23 U.S.C. 161 (zero tolerance requirement); state driver manuals

q: What does implied consent mean?
a: You may refuse any test without penalty
b: Police need your written consent before any test
c: You agree to a test only if you have been in a crash
d: By driving, you have agreed to a chemical test if police lawfully ask
exp: Accepting a license means you agreed in advance to breath, blood or urine testing when an officer suspects impaired driving.
src: State driver manuals, implied consent section

q: You are driving on a highway and keep yawning, and you cannot remember the last few miles. What should you do?
a: Open the window and keep driving
b: Turn up the radio
c: Pull off at a safe place and rest
d: Drink a cup of coffee and keep going
exp: These are warning signs of drowsy driving. The only real fix is rest, so stop at a safe place.
src: https://www.nhtsa.gov/risky-driving/drowsy-driving

q: Which driving ability does alcohol affect first, often before the drinker feels drunk?
a: Judgment
b: Reaction time
c: Vision
d: Coordination
exp: Alcohol dulls judgment first, which is why people who have been drinking often decide they are fine to drive.
src: NHTSA, Drunk Driving (effects of BAC); state driver manuals, alcohol section

q: Your allergy medicine label says it may cause drowsiness. What should you do?
a: Avoid driving until you know how it affects you
b: Drink coffee and drive
c: Drive, because it is a legal medicine
d: Drive, but only on short trips near home
exp: Legal medicines can impair you, and driving impaired by any drug is illegal. Check the label and find out how it affects you first.
src: NHTSA, Drug Impaired Driving; state driver manuals

q: Which of these drinks holds about the same amount of alcohol as 12 ounces of regular beer?
a: A 12 ounce glass of wine
b: Two 1.5 ounce shots of liquor
c: A 1.5 ounce shot of 80 proof liquor
d: A 24 ounce can of malt liquor
exp: A standard drink is 12 ounces of beer, 5 ounces of wine or 1.5 ounces of 80 proof liquor. Each holds about the same alcohol.
src: https://www.niaaa.nih.gov/alcohols-effects-health/what-standard-drink

q: What are the three kinds of driver distraction?
a: Physical, emotional and mental
b: Hearing, seeing and feeling
c: Passenger, phone and radio
d: Visual, manual and cognitive
exp: Distractions take your eyes off the road (visual), your hands off the wheel (manual) or your mind off driving (cognitive).
src: CDC, Distracted Driving; state driver manuals

q: About how long can you stay awake before your driving is impaired about as much as with a BAC of 0.05?
a: About 8 hours
b: About 18 hours
c: About 12 hours
d: About 36 hours
exp: Being awake about 18 hours impairs you about as much as a 0.05 BAC, and 24 hours about as much as 0.10.
src: CDC, Drowsy Driving: Asleep at the Wheel; CDC NIOSH, Driver Fatigue on the Job

q: What does BAC stand for?
a: Breath alcohol count
b: Basic alcohol check
c: Blood alcohol concentration
d: Blood absorption control
exp: BAC is the share of alcohol in your blood, measured by a breath, blood or urine test.
src: https://www.nhtsa.gov/risky-driving/drunk-driving

q: Under federal rules, what BAC limit applies to a person driving a commercial vehicle?
exp: Commercial drivers are held to 0.04, half the 0.08 limit for other drivers 21 and older.
src: 49 CFR 382.201 and 383.51 (FMCSA, 0.04 BAC for commercial drivers)

q: Two friends each drink the same amount in the same hour. Which one is likely to reach the higher BAC?
a: The one who drank beer instead of liquor
b: The one who drank more water afterward
c: The one who is taller but weighs the same
d: The one who weighs less
exp: Body size matters: a smaller person reaches a higher BAC from the same amount of alcohol.
src: State driver manuals, factors affecting BAC
